pageDescription: How each part of the dashboard works.
managementApiHeading: Managing the section over the API
outgoingFormatsNote: Every outgoing webhook has a delivery format, chosen in <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing>. “Inspoter” is our own envelope signed with HMAC-SHA256. “Discord” posts the event as an embed card straight into a Discord channel: point it at a Discord webhook URL and nothing else is needed. “Discord Webhook Events” suits receivers written against Discord: an envelope signed with Ed25519, with the verifying public key shown alongside.
dashboardsCardDescription: Build your own overview from widgets — clock, weather, calendar, and data from any section.
dashboardsIntroP1: Dashboards are named overview pages inside a workspace. Each one holds widgets: global ones (clock and date, weather, calendar, note) and ones that read a section — bookmarks, service status, server metrics, mail, messages, alerts, and logs.
dashboardsIntroP2: Widgets sit on a 12-column grid and can be dragged and resized, but only in edit mode — in normal mode the tiles stay interactive and never move on a stray press. Widget data refreshes itself once a minute while the page is open. Dashboards are shared across the workspace, and one of them can be made the start page, which is what opens right after signing in.
dashboardsSteps: Choose “New dashboard” from the actions menu and give it a name — for example “Production” or “On call”.
Click “Edit”, then “Add widget”, and pick a type from the catalogue.
The widget's settings open right after it is added: that is where you set weather coordinates, a bookmark category, a specific server or mailbox, how many entries to show, and a custom title.
In edit mode, drag a widget by the handle on the left of its header, and resize it from the grip in the bottom-right corner — with the grip focused, the arrow keys resize it a cell at a time.
Click “Done” to leave edit mode: widgets then show a link into their section instead of the actions menu.
The dashboard menu renames it, makes it the start page, or deletes it — deleting a dashboard never touches section data.
bookmarksCardDescription: Organize saved links into categories and subcategories.
bookmarksIntroP1: Bookmarks stores links to sites and tools you use often, grouped into categories with one level of subcategories. Each bookmark can have a name, URL, description, and icon.
bookmarksIntroP2: Categories and bookmarks can be reordered by drag-and-drop, and the whole library can be searched or filtered by category.
bookmarksSteps: Click "New category" to create a top-level category, or add a subcategory from an existing category's menu.
Inside a category, click "Add" to create a bookmark with a name, URL, description, and icon.
Drag a category header or bookmark card to reorder it; drag a bookmark onto another category to move it there.
Use the search box to filter by name, description, or URL, and the category dropdown to show only one category.
Use a category's or bookmark's menu to rename or delete it — deleting a category also deletes its bookmarks.
bookmarksManagementApiIntro: Bookmarks can also be searched and managed by an external system or an AI assistant. Grant a token the Bookmarks permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>: the same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP, where an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
bookmarksManagementApiFields: bookmarks:read — search bookmarks and list categories.
bookmarks:write — create, update, delete and reorder bookmarks and categories.
Deleting a category is deliberately absent from the API: it takes every bookmark inside it with it, so that stays an operator action in the interface.
kanbanCardDescription: Track work on drag-and-drop boards with columns, checklists and comments.
kanbanIntroP1: Kanban holds any number of boards, each with columns you define — for example To do, Doing, Done — and cards that move between them. A card carries a title, description, priority, due date, an assignee from the workspace, and colored labels.
kanbanIntroP2: A card can also link to a server, domain, service, alert or hosting account, so the board doubles as a task list tied to the infrastructure it is about. Mark one column terminal and dropping a card into it marks the card complete.
kanbanSteps: Click "New board" to create a board, then "Add column" to lay out its stages.
Click "Add card" in a column to create a card with a title, priority and due date.
Drag a card between columns to move it, or within a column to reorder it; dropping it into the terminal column (marked Done) completes the card.
Open a card to add a checklist, leave comments, assign it to a workspace member, attach labels, or link it to a server, domain, service, alert or hosting account.
Use "Manage labels" to create colored labels shared across the board's cards.
Use a board's, column's or card's menu to rename or delete it — deleting a board or column also deletes the cards inside it.
kanbanManagementApiIntro: Boards can also be read and managed by an external system or an AI assistant. Grant a token the Kanban permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>: the same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP, where an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
kanbanManagementApiFields: kanban:read — list boards, search cards, and read checklists, comments and labels.
kanban:write — create and update boards, columns, cards, checklists, comments and labels, and move cards between columns.
Deleting a board or a column is deliberately absent from the API: either takes every card inside it with it, so that stays an operator action in the interface.
A comment posted by a token is signed with the token's name, and only that same token can delete it again.
kanbanOutgoingWebhook: Kanban has no incoming webhook — cards are created from the interface or through the API above. Moving a card does fire outgoing events, though: KANBAN_CARD_CREATED, KANBAN_CARD_MOVED and, when a card lands in the terminal column, KANBAN_CARD_COMPLETED. Subscribe an external URL to any of them under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing> to forward them to a chat, pager, or automation.
domainsCardDescription: View and manage DNS records across connected providers.
domainsIntroP1: Domains lists every domain from your connected DNS providers (Cloudflare, Hetzner DNS, GoDaddy) in one table, with the number of DNS records and which provider manages it.
domainsIntroP2: From a domain you can drill into its DNS records, or link it to an existing Bookmark or Service — or create one pre-filled with the domain's name.
domainsSteps: Click "Add provider" to connect a Cloudflare, Hetzner DNS, or GoDaddy API credential.
The table lists every domain across providers, with its DNS record count and provider badge.
Click "View DNS records" on a domain to see and edit its DNS records.
Use the row's link menu to create or open a linked Bookmark or Service for that domain.
If a provider shows an error banner, click "Retry" to re-fetch it live.
serversCardDescription: Monitor and control servers from cloud providers and the metrics agent.
serversIntroP1: Servers shows every server from your connected cloud providers alongside any host running the InSpoter metrics agent, combined into one card per server.
serversIntroP2: Each card shows live status, CPU/RAM/disk usage, OS, location, and uptime, and — where the provider supports it — Start/Stop/Restart controls.
serversSteps: Click "Add provider" to connect a server-hosting provider credential.
Each card shows status, CPU/RAM/disk usage (from the metrics agent if installed, otherwise the provider's plan capacity), OS, location, and uptime.
Use the Start, Stop, or Restart buttons (with a confirmation dialog) to control provider-managed servers.
Click "Refresh" to force a live re-fetch of every provider instead of the cached snapshot.
For a server without live metrics, click "Set up monitoring" to enroll it with the metrics agent.
serversWebhookIntro: Live metrics arrive over HTTP as well, but the body is assembled by the InSpoter metrics agent rather than by hand: install it with "Set up monitoring" on a server card, give it an API token from <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>, and it posts CPU, memory, disk, and uptime on its own schedule. Each submission is matched to a server by the IP addresses the agent reports. The endpoint is described in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
hostingCardDescription: Track shared hosting accounts across connected providers.
hostingIntroP1: Hosting aggregates shared-hosting/control-panel accounts from your connected providers into one card grid, showing domain, plan, and status.
hostingIntroP2: Each card reports disk and bandwidth usage, database and e-mail account counts, and — for supported providers — lets you suspend or unsuspend the account.
hostingSteps: Click "Add provider" to connect a hosting-panel API credential.
Each card shows the account's domain, status, disk and bandwidth usage with meters, database and e-mail counts, and plan.
Where supported, use Suspend/Unsuspend (with a confirmation dialog) to change the account's state.
Click "Refresh" to force a live re-fetch; a failing provider shows a retry banner.
servicesCardDescription: Uptime monitoring for HTTP, TCP, and PING targets.
servicesIntroP1: Services runs uptime checks against HTTP, TCP, or PING targets you define, polling on the interval you set and recording a status history for each.
servicesIntroP2: Every card auto-refreshes roughly every 10 seconds and shows the current status, last check time, response time, and a heartbeat strip of recent checks.
servicesSteps: Click "New service" to add an HTTP, TCP, or PING monitor with its target address and check interval.
Each card auto-refreshes and shows a status badge, last-checked time, response time, and a heartbeat strip of recent checks.
Click "Check now" to force an immediate check outside the regular interval.
Use Pause/Resume to stop or restart monitoring without deleting the service.
Use "Manage labels" to create labels, then the search box and label filter to narrow the list.
Click a card's title to open its detail page, or use the card menu to edit or delete it.
servicesManagementApiIntro: Services can also be created and managed by an external system or an AI assistant — defining a monitor, pausing it, or triggering a check on demand. Grant a token the Services permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>: the same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP, where an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
servicesManagementApiFields: services:read — list and read monitored services, their check history, and labels.
services:write — create, update, delete, pause or resume a service, check it on demand, and manage labels.
servicesOutgoingWebhook: Services have no incoming webhook — the dashboard runs the checks itself. Status changes do fire a SERVICE_STATUS event outwards, though: subscribe an external URL to it under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing> to forward them to a chat, pager, or automation.
mailCardDescription: A three-pane webmail client for connected IMAP accounts.
mailIntroP1: Mail is a three-pane webmail client — accounts and folders on the left, the message list in the middle, and the reading pane on the right — for IMAP/SMTP mailboxes you connect, plus a built-in webhook mailbox for mail received over the API.
mailIntroP2: You can search, filter to unread, sort, reply/forward/archive/delete, apply labels, and set up filter rules that automatically label future incoming mail.
mailSteps: Click "Add account" to connect an IMAP/SMTP mailbox.
Pick an account and folder in the sidebar, then use search, "Unread only", and sort to narrow the message list.
Click a message to read it, and use Reply, Forward, Archive, Delete, or mark read/unread from the reading pane.
Click "Sync" to pull new mail from the server on demand.
Use "Manage labels" to create colored labels and apply them to messages, and "Filter rules" to auto-label future mail matching a sender or subject.
Click "Compose" to write new mail; unsent drafts are saved and reopened from the Drafts folder.
mailWebhookIntro: Besides IMAP accounts, mail can be pushed in over HTTP: the message lands in the Inbox of the built-in webhook mailbox, with no mail server involved. Authenticate with an API token from <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens> and POST a JSON body; the full contract is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
mailWebhookFields: receivedAt — optional: ISO 8601 date-time; defaults to the moment the request arrives.
mailManagementApiIntro: The webhook above only delivers a single message into the built-in webhook mailbox. When an external system or an AI assistant should work an IMAP mailbox instead — search and read mail, send and file drafts, apply labels, manage filter rules, and trigger a sync — grant a token the Mail permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>. The same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP, where an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
mailManagementApiFields: mail:read — search and read mail, folders, labels, filter rules and attachments.
mail:write — mark read, move, delete, label, send, save drafts, manage filter rules and labels, and trigger a sync.

Creating, editing, deleting or testing a mail account is deliberately absent from the API — that would put a password through the token's context, so accounts stay an operator action in Settings → Mail.
mailOutgoingWebhook: Mail arriving in a mailbox also fires a MAIL_RECEIVED event outwards — subscribe an external URL to it under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing>.
messagesCardDescription: Slack-style channels for internal chat and incoming webhooks.
messagesIntroP1: Messages organizes channels into categories, similar to Slack, for both manual team chat and messages posted in by external systems through a channel's webhook.
messagesIntroP2: Select a channel to see its timeline, scroll up to load older history, and send messages from the composer at the bottom.
messagesSteps: Use the sidebar's "+" controls to create a category, then a channel inside it.
Select a channel to view its message timeline; scroll up or click "Load previous" for older messages.
Type in the composer and send to post a message to the selected channel.
Open a channel's settings (gear icon) to rename it or manage its incoming webhook, used by external systems to post into it.
Use the category or channel context menu to rename or delete it.
messagesWebhookIntro: External systems can post into a channel two ways. A channel webhook, created from the channel's settings (gear icon), gets its own URL with the credential built into it and needs no token header and no channelId — treat that URL as a password and keep it out of logs and screenshots. A workspace API token from <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens> instead posts to the shared endpoint below and names the target channel in the body. Both are described in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
messagesWebhookFields: channelId — required: internal id of the target channel; it is not shown in the interface, which is why a channel webhook is usually the easier route.
content — required: the message text, up to 4000 characters.
author — optional: the sender name shown in the timeline; defaults to the webhook's name.
messagesDiscordIntro: A channel webhook also understands Discord's format. If an integration already posts to a Discord channel — CI, Grafana, Sentry, Uptime Kuma, GitHub Actions — just point it at the Discord-compatible URL instead of the discord.com link: the request body needs no rewriting. The address is revealed once in the channel settings dialog next to the native one and carries the same secret, so handle it just as carefully. The full specification with limits and error codes lives in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
messagesDiscordFields: content — the message text, up to 2000 characters.
embeds — up to 10 cards with a colour bar, title, description and fields. At most 6000 characters across all of them.
username — the sender name; the webhook's own name is used when it is absent.
avatar_url — the sender avatar shown beside the message.
The default response is 204 with no body, as on Discord. Add ?wait=true to get 200 and the created message object.
Errors use Discord's shape: 50006 for an empty message, 50035 for a broken limit, 401 for an unknown or revoked webhook, and 429 with retry_after when the rate limit is hit.
The /slack suffix accepts Slack's format: text and attachments become the message text and cards.
File attachments are accepted but not stored; threads, components and polls are ignored.
messagesManagementApiIntro: The webhooks above only write into a channel that already exists. When an external system or an AI assistant should lay out the section itself — create categories and channels, wire up webhooks and post into them — grant a token the Messages permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>. The same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP: an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
messagesManagementApiFields: The permissions split in two: "Search and read" grants reading only, while "Manage and post" is required for every change and for issuing channel webhooks.
Creating a category or a channel is idempotent: repeating the request with the same name (case is ignored) returns the existing record instead of duplicating it.
Messages posted with a token are labelled "Agent" in the timeline and authored by the token's name, so it is clear a human did not write them.
Deleting categories and channels is deliberately absent from the API: a category takes its whole message history with it, so that stays an operator action in the interface.

Errors come back as {"error":{"code","message"}}: 401 when the token is missing or revoked, 403 when a permission is lacking, 404 when the object is not in your workspace, and 429 when the rate limit is hit.
messagesOutgoingWebhook: Every posted message also fires a MESSAGE_CREATED event outwards — subscribe an external URL to it under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing>.
activityCardDescription: Audit log of every action taken in the workspace.
activityIntroP1: Activity is a read-only audit trail of every create, update, delete, and other action operators take across the workspace — bookmarks, domains, servers, mail, tokens, and more.
activityIntroP2: Entries are searchable and filterable, and each row can be expanded to see the full details of what changed.
activitySteps: Use the search box, and the Action, Entity type, and Operator filters to narrow the table.
Use the sort control to switch between newest-first and oldest-first.
Click the chevron on a row with details to expand its full change payload.
Use Previous/Next to page through history.
logsCardDescription: Central log collector fed by the incoming webhook API.
logsIntroP1: Logs stores log lines pushed in by external systems through the log webhook endpoint, so scripts, cron jobs, and services outside InSpoter have one place to report what they did.
logsIntroP2: Entries are searchable and filterable by level and source, and each row can be expanded to see its full message and details.
logsSteps: Point an external system at the log webhook endpoint with a bearer token to start sending entries (see the example request shown when the list is empty).
Use the search box, Level filter, and Source filter to narrow the list.
Use the sort control to switch between newest-first and oldest-first.
Click the chevron on a row to expand its full message and details.
Use Previous/Next to page through results.
logsWebhookIntro: Any script, cron job, or service can push entries in over HTTP. Create an API token under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>, send it in the Authorization header, and POST a JSON body to the log endpoint. The full contract is also available in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
logsWebhookFields: level — required: severity of the entry, for example info, warn, or error.
source — required: what produced the entry, for example backup.sh or api-gateway.
message — required: the log line itself.
timestamp — optional: ISO 8601 date-time; defaults to the moment the request arrives.
logsOutgoingWebhook: Every new entry also fires a LOG_CREATED event outwards — subscribe an external URL to it under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing>.
alertsCardDescription: Categorized alert inbox fed by the incoming webhook API.
alertsIntroP1: Alerts stores alert events pushed in by external systems through the alert webhook endpoint, organized into categories you define (e.g. "Deploy", "Security") with an info/warning/error/critical severity.
alertsIntroP2: Entries are searchable and filterable by category and severity, so you can triage what needs attention.
alertsSteps: Click "New category" to define alert categories used to classify incoming alerts.
Point an external system at the alert webhook endpoint with a bearer token, including category, severity, source, and message (see the example request shown when the list is empty).
Use the search box, Category filter, and Severity filter to narrow the table.
Use the sort control and Previous/Next to page through results.
Use "Manage categories" to rename or delete alert categories.
alertsWebhookIntro: Alerts arrive the same way log entries do: an API token from <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens> in the Authorization header plus a JSON POST. The category is matched by name and created automatically when it does not exist yet, so a monitoring system can send its own labels without setting them up first. The full contract is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
alertsWebhookFields: category — required: category name; created automatically if there is no such category yet.
severity — required: info, warning, error, or critical.
source — required: what raised the alert.
timestamp — optional: ISO 8601 date-time; defaults to the moment the request arrives.
alertsOutgoingWebhook: Every alert also fires an ALERT_CREATED event outwards — subscribe an external URL to it under <outgoing>Settings → Outgoing webhooks</outgoing>.
contactsCardDescription: A shared address book with labels, import, export, and duplicate merging.
contactsIntroP1: Contacts is the workspace address book: one row per person or organization, each holding as many emails, phone numbers, addresses, chat handles, dates and related people as it needs.
contactsIntroP2: It reads and writes the formats every other address book speaks — vCard 2.1/3.0/4.0, Google CSV, Outlook CSV and Thunderbird LDIF — so moving a book in or out is a single file, and it finds contacts that describe the same person so you can merge them.
contactsSteps: Click "New contact" to add someone by hand; every detail row can carry its own label.
Use "Import" to load a vCard, CSV or LDIF file, and choose what should happen when a contact already exists.
Search by name, email, phone or organization; the search box also matches a phone number typed without its spaces.
Use "Manage labels" to create colored labels, then apply them from a contact or from the list selection.
Star the people you reach for often to keep them under "Starred".
Open "Merge duplicates" to review contacts that share an address, a number or a name, and fold them into one.
Use "Export" to write the current filter, the current selection, or the whole book out in any supported format.
contactsManagementApiIntro: Contacts can also be read and written by an external system or an AI assistant. Grant a token the Contacts permissions under <tokens>Settings → Webhooks</tokens>: the same token works over plain REST (sample below) and over MCP, where an assistant such as Claude or Cursor connects to /api/mcp and gets the same operations as tools. The full route list is in <apiDocs>Settings → API Documentation</apiDocs>.
contactsManagementApiFields: contacts:read — list and read contacts and labels.
contacts:write — create, update and delete contacts, and import a vCard.
